summary:
EarthWatch is a browser-based Earth observation explorer that turns NASA satellite imagery into an interactive 3D globe. Instead of a flat map or a static chart, users spin a live planet and toggle environmental layers like NDVI (vegetation greenness), surface pressure, soil moisture, CO₂ concentration, and sea level change, to see how land, atmosphere, and oceans shift over time. The app pulls public NASA GIBS imagery, drapes it on a Three.js globe, and lets people scrub dates, compare seasons, highlight vegetation “bloom,” extrude pressure into height, and sample any point for a plain-language reading, without downloading raw files or writing code.

This matters because Earth trends are usually locked in specialist tools, Jupyter notebooks, or Earth Engine scripts. EarthWatch makes the same public NASA products explorable in one page: no API key for the core globe, no install step, and a workflow that is visual first—menu → layer → timeline → sample—so students, interns, and researchers can spot vegetation pulses, dry soils, CO₂ patterns, pressure systems, and sea level signals quickly and share them as a living demo rather than a screenshot.
details:
EarthWatch is a front-end Earth visualization app focused on time-aware satellite layers on a globe. The system requests equirectangular PNG composites from NASA’s Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS) WMS for a chosen date, loads them as textures in Three.js, and wraps them on spheres slightly larger than a Blue Marble base Earth.

Current layers include:

  • NDVI — MODIS Terra 8-day vegetation index, with month-to-month crossfade and an optional bloom shader for places greener than the prior month
  • Surface pressure — MERRA-2 monthly pressure, with a custom shader that can extrude lows and highs into 3D height
  • Soil moisture — satellite soil moisture browse imagery for wet vs dry land patterns
  • CO₂ concentration — atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration maps for spatial greenhouse-gas context
  • Sea level change — ocean height / sea level trend imagery to show coastal and basin-scale change

A left-side menu switches layers; a bottom dock controls playback, layer-specific tools (such as Bloom and Extrude), Spin, and a date scrubber. Hover raycasting samples pixels and classifies them into readable categories shown in the info card and legend for each active layer.

The benefit is accessibility with honest presentation: EarthWatch uses NASA’s published color imagery and clear legends rather than inventing exact geophysical numbers from RGB alone. The intended impact is a lightweight, shareable way to explore multiple Earth systems in one globe—for education, demos, and early analysis—with a clear path to add more GIBS layers by swapping the layer name and legend.

We built the project as a single-page app with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript modules, Three.js (WebGL globe, OrbitControls, shaders), and NASA GIBS WMS. Hosting is static; the GitHub repo is the source of truth for the current build.

The project is creative because it treats satellite “browse” imagery as a first-class interactive medium: not a dashboard of charts, but a planet you can spin, layer, and query by point across vegetation, soil, carbon, atmosphere, and sea level. We optimized for clarity over spectacle—solid UI panels, readable typography, and layer toggles that hide data until asked—so the globe stays the focus.
